extracted.intended_audience: university students and tutors (especially those studying or teaching Latin composition and preparing for university examinations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for university-level students and tutors on preparing for university examinations and on writing good Latin (translation and composition), including principles of idiom, structure, and essay/Theme-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of vocabulary (diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the four requisites of good Composition—correctness of vocabulary, or diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a basic requisite likely to be displayed by every candidate. Use classical words; be aware that correct diction alone does not guarantee idiomatic or Latinate style (see idiom and structure). Examples in the text show literal translations that are dictionally correct yet fail to be Latin in style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the four requisites of good Composition—correctness of syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grammatical constructions must be correct. However, purely grammatical (syntactically correct) sentences can still be un-Latin in idiom and structure. The author warns that exact acquaintance with grammar and dictionary is necessary but insufficient for good composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiomatic propriety (idiom)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the four requisites of good Composition—idiomatic propriety: the particular use of words and constructions peculiar to a language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition and extensive guidance: idiom = the use of words peculiar to a language; literal, word-for-word translations that follow English idiom produce correct diction and syntax but 'Latinity it simply has none.' Anti-patterns: translating English expressions literally into Latin (Anglicism). The text gives a full worked example (literal rendering of English about 'taste of blood') and enumerates specific points to watch: (1) Latin has no articles (use quidam or other devices), (2) consideratio often denotes the act, not 'a consideration' as an object, (3) many Latin words are metaphorical and cannot be used simply, (4) English may throw two ideas together which must be separated in Latin, (5) 'inter' is not the simple Latin for 'among' (use 'in' for simple 'among'), (6) active indicatives followed by accusatives are generally foreign to Latin sentence-structure, (7) Latin prefers carrying on the same subject across connected clauses, (8) 'et' may not be the best connector for distinct clauses—'autem' often preferable. The paper also shows progressive pupil translations to illustrate moving from Anglicism toward Latinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the four requisites of good Composition—elegance (desirable but not essential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance of style is desirable but not essential for examination success; correctness and idiomatic propriety take precedence. Elegance can be cultivated but should not replace clarity, structure, and idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for the particular character of the examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates should direct efforts to distinct preparation for the examination's particular character; 'do a little well' rather than spreading effort thinly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice to parents/students: understand the specific demands of your university's examination and prepare accordingly. Rather than attempting a very wide 'general' reading, the rule recommended is to prepare a limited field thoroughly. Options: postpone residence and study specifically for six months; attend a good school or engage a private tutor to drill on the exam's style and requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be well grounded; cultivate accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be 'well grounded' and cultivate accuracy—avoid vagueness and superficial breadth without depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation that youths commonly lack accuracy; tutors should aim to ground students in essentials. The tutor's diagnosis: candidate 'knows something about a great many things' but lacks exactness; remedy is focused, accurate study rather than desultory reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of general knowledge vs. examination-specific technicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasting view: general knowledge (substance) is more valuable for 'the world' than narrow technicalities of examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Brown's argument: general knowledge fits a youth for practical life; substance of knowledge is more valuable than technical minutiae. He believes vigor of youthful mind should not be wasted on 'barren learning' and that being 'up to the world's requisitions' requires broad reading. This is presented as a legitimate, alternative standard to strict exam-focused preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to the thesis / keep to the subject in Themes
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing Themes/essays, adhere closely to the thesis and avoid running off into irrelevant generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Black criticizes a pupil who ignored the thesis 'Fortes fortuna adjuvat' and wandered into generalities about 'fortune.' Practical rules: interpret the thesis as a guide; choose a definite, narrow formulation (e.g., 'Fortune favours the bold') to steady the composition; avoid starting from a false point or rambling through unrelated examples. Anti-patterns: treating a vague word ('fortune') as the subject and attempting to cover all aspects at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a definite subject and be precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer definite, limited subjects over vague, all-encompassing ones; precision steadies and guides writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: give students a specific, manageable topic or thesis to focus on; vague subjects lead to inaccuracy and rambling. Example: choose 'Fortune favours the bold' rather than 'fortune' in general. This aids in producing connected, consequential detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think before you write; avoid empty composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule: first think, then write; do not write when you have nothing to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thoughtful youth may write little but better quality work than one who writes a large quantity of empty sentences. Anti-patterns listed include reliance on 'flowers, full-blown flowers, figures, smart expressions, trite quotations, hackneyed beginnings and endings, pompous circumlocutions' rather than solid sense and foundation. The examiner values sense and structure over ornate phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure is the turning-point of good Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Latinity lies primarily in structure: how the sentence is organized (carrying subject, clause structure, resolution of abstract nouns, placement of verb), not merely in choice of elegant words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Black's experience: mere accumulation of classical words and idioms without understanding sentence-structure yields poor Latinity. Structural features to attend to include: carrying one subject/nominative across connected clauses, breaking a sentence into appropriate clauses, evasion of categorical forms when Latin requires different construction, converting abstract nouns into verbs/participles where Latin prefers, appropriate placement of the verb (e.g., end-placement tendencies), and compensating for lack of brevity by elegance while maintaining perspicuity. The author recommends studying Cicero and other exemplars to induce structural principles and to record peculiarities systematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use models and induction from exemplary authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn Latinity by close study and induction from classical models (e.g., Cicero) and from carefully edited modern Latin lectures; note peculiarities and make rules from examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: keep blank books noting peculiarities of sentences, force of words, collocations, carrying of subject, clause resolution, etc.; use examples as patterns to copy and improve. Avoid relying purely on formulaic memorization of phrases; instead use models to induce the underlying principles of style and structure. The text contrasts copying phrases (making 'bricks') with using authors as a 'capital' to improve.
